question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The toddler decided to make a mess because he wanted to ______ the attention of its parents.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. seek.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Seek" means to try to get or obtain something; to look for. The collocation "seek attention" is the fixed, natural expression in English for trying to draw notice to oneself. (ध्यान आकर्षित करने का प्रयास करना)

◦ Correct: The toddler decided to make a mess because he wanted to seek the attention of its parents.

• A child creating a mess deliberately is classic "attention-seeking" behaviour, so "seek" fits both the grammar and the meaning perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "elicit" means to draw out a response, reaction or information from someone (elicit a reply / elicit information). One elicits a reaction, not "attention" — the collocation is wrong.

• Option 3 "please" means to give satisfaction or pleasure to someone. "Please the attention" is meaningless; you please a person, not an abstract noun like attention.

• Option 4 "extract" means to pull or take out by force (extract a tooth / extract a confession). It carries a sense of force that does not suit "attention".

NOTE

• Common collocations with "attention": seek attention, pay attention, draw attention, attract attention, divert attention, bring to one's attention.

• Useful derivatives: seeker (noun — one who seeks), sought (past/past participle of seek). Remember the irregular form: seek – sought – sought.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Glimpse
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Glance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Glimpse" means a very brief, quick or partial look at something. Its closest synonym is "glance", which also means a quick, hurried look. (झलक / एक क्षणिक दृष्टि)

◦ Example: I caught a glimpse of the actor as his car sped past.

◦ Example: She threw a quick glance at her watch.

• Both words share the key idea of shortness of duration — the look lasts only a moment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Examine" means to inspect closely and in detail — the opposite of a hurried look.

• Option 3 "Stare" means to look fixedly for a long time, often rudely; it is a prolonged look, not a brief one.

• Option 4 "Observe" means to watch carefully and attentively, usually over a period of time, in order to notice something.

NOTE

• Synonyms of glimpse: glance, peek, peep, sighting, brief look. Antonyms: gaze, stare, gape, contemplate.

• Remember the family of "looking" words graded by duration: glimpse/glance (a second) → look (brief) → watch/observe (sustained) → stare/gaze (long and fixed) → scrutinise/examine (long and detailed).

question: Identify the sentence that contains correct spellings in the given context.
option_1: She acid the test despite being sleep-deprived from studying for nearly 24 hours straight.
option_2: She acad the test desspite being sleep-deprived from studying for nearly 24 hours straight.
option_3: She aced the test daspite being sleep-deprived from studying for nearly 24 hours strait.
option_4: She aced the test despite being sleep-deprived from studying for nearly 24 hours straight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. She aced the test despite being sleep-deprived from studying for nearly 24 hours straight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Three words decide this question, and only Option 4 spells all three correctly:

◦ "aced" — the verb "to ace (a test)" means to pass with flying colours / score very highly. (परीक्षा में शानदार प्रदर्शन करना)

◦ "despite" — a preposition meaning in spite of; notwithstanding. It is written as ONE word with a single "s": DE + SPITE.

◦ "straight" — meaning continuously, without a break ("24 hours straight").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 wrongly uses "acid" (an acid is a sour chemical substance) instead of "aced".

• Option 2 has two errors — "acad" (not a word) and "desspite" (double "s" is wrong).

• Option 3 has two errors — "daspite" (wrong vowel) and "strait" (a strait is a narrow channel of water, e.g., the Palk Strait; it does not mean "continuously").

NOTE

• Watch the classic homophone pair: straight (not bent / continuously) vs strait (a narrow sea passage; also "dire straits" = serious difficulty).

• "Despite" and "in spite of" are followed by a noun or gerund, never by a clause: despite being tired (✓), despite he was tired (✗).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The teacher assured: “You have completed your homework, __________?”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. haven’t you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is a question tag. The rule is: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and the tag must repeat the same auxiliary verb and the same subject (as a pronoun) used in the statement.

◦ Statement: "You have completed your homework" — positive, auxiliary = have, subject = you.

◦ Therefore the tag must be the negative of "have" with "you": "haven't you?"

◦ Correct: You have completed your homework, haven't you?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "had you" and Option 2 "hadn't you" use the wrong auxiliary — the sentence uses the present perfect "have completed", not the past perfect "had completed".

• Option 4 "have you" is positive, but a positive statement requires a negative tag.

NOTE

• Question-tag rules for SSC:

◦ Positive statement → negative tag: She is coming, isn't she?

◦ Negative statement → positive tag: He didn't call, did he?

◦ Imperative → will you / won't you: Open the door, will you?

◦ "Let's ..." → shall we: Let's go, shall we?

◦ "I am ..." → aren't I: I am right, aren't I?

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word given in brackets to fill in the blank.

A _________________(distinct) sense of restlessness was bothering me when I left the cemetery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. vague.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Distinct" means clear, definite, easily noticed and unmistakable. Its antonym is "vague", meaning unclear, indefinite, not sharply defined. (स्पष्ट का विलोम — अस्पष्ट / धुंधला)

◦ Correct: A vague sense of restlessness was bothering me when I left the cemetery.

• A "vague sense of restlessness" is also the natural collocation — an uneasy feeling one cannot pin down.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "terrible" (very bad, dreadful) is not the opposite of "distinct".

• Option 2 "critical" (crucial / fault-finding) is unrelated to clarity.

• Option 3 "prior" (earlier, previous) refers to time, not to clarity.

NOTE

• Synonyms of distinct: clear, definite, evident, marked, unmistakable, discernible. Antonyms: vague, indistinct, hazy, obscure, blurred.

• Do not confuse distinct (clear/separate) with distinctive (characteristic, serving to identify) — a distinct smell vs a distinctive uniform.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.

With cloud streaming, people can play games from a / internet-connected device, avoiding the need for pricey / dedicated hardware such as a game console.
option_2: dedicated hardware such as a game console
option_3: With cloud streaming, people can play games from a
option_4: internet-connected device, avoiding the need for pricey
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. With cloud streaming, people can play games from a.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error is the article "a". The word that follows is "internet-connected device", which begins with the vowel sound /ɪ/. Before a vowel sound we must use "an", not "a".

◦ Correct: With cloud streaming, people can play games from an internet-connected device, avoiding the need for pricey dedicated hardware such as a game console.

• The choice between a and an depends on the SOUND that follows, not on the letter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Part "internet-connected device, avoiding the need for pricey" is correct — "pricey" (expensive) is a proper adjective and the participle phrase "avoiding ..." is correctly used.

• Part "dedicated hardware such as a game console" is correct — "hardware" is an uncountable noun and "such as" correctly introduces an example.

NOTE

• Article rules by sound:

◦ an before vowel sounds: an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an heir, an umbrella.

◦ a before consonant sounds even if the word starts with a vowel letter: a university, a European, a one-rupee coin, a useful book.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Keep someone at arm’s length
option_2: To avoid becoming too close or friendly with someone
option_4: Having energy again after being tired
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To avoid becoming too close or friendly with someone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "keep someone at arm's length" means to avoid becoming too friendly or intimate with someone; to maintain a deliberate distance. The image is of literally holding a person as far away as your arm can reach. (किसी से दूरी बनाए रखना)

◦ Example: Ever since the quarrel, she has kept her cousin at arm's length.

◦ Example: Wise investors keep dubious schemes at arm's length.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "to ruin someone's plans" is the meaning of idioms like "upset the applecart" or "put a spanner in the works".

• Option 3 "angry about something" corresponds to "hot under the collar" or "see red".

• Option 4 "having energy again after being tired" corresponds to "get a second wind" or "recharge one's batteries".

NOTE

• Related expressions: an "arm's-length transaction" in business/law means a deal between parties who are independent of each other, with no special relationship.

• Similar distance idioms: "give someone a wide berth" (avoid someone), "steer clear of" (stay away from).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains an error.

(A) This fridge / (B) comes including / (C) a 5-year / (D) warranty.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. B.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part (B) "comes including" is wrong. When a product is sold together with something, the correct expression is "comes with". "Including" is a preposition used to show that something is part of a larger group ("the bill, including taxes"), and it cannot follow "comes" in this sense.

◦ Correct: This fridge comes with a 5-year warranty.

• "Come with" is the standard collocation for accompanying features/accessories: The phone comes with a charger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Part (A) "This fridge" is correct — a singular demonstrative + singular noun.

• Part (C) "a 5-year" is correct — when a number + noun works as a compound adjective before a noun, the noun stays singular and hyphenated: a 5-year warranty, a 10-rupee note, a three-hour meeting.

• Part (D) "warranty" is correctly spelt and correctly used.

NOTE

• Useful phrasal patterns: come with (be supplied along with), come across (find by chance), come by (obtain), come up with (produce an idea), come round (regain consciousness / change one's opinion).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

One who looks at the dark side of life
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pessimist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "pessimist" is a person who always looks at the dark/gloomy side of things and expects the worst to happen. (निराशावादी)

◦ Example: A pessimist sees difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees opportunity in every difficulty.

• The word comes from the Latin pessimus meaning "worst".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Physicist" — a person who specialises in physics (unrelated).

• Option 2 "Optimist" — a person who looks at the bright side of life and hopes for the best; this is the exact opposite of the required word.

• Option 4 "Idealist" — a person guided by ideals rather than practical considerations.

NOTE

• Frequently asked one-word substitutes of this family: Optimist (hopeful person), Pessimist (gloomy person), Realist (one who accepts things as they are), Cynic (one who distrusts others' motives), Misanthrope (one who hates mankind), Philanthropist (one who loves and helps mankind), Egotist (one who talks constantly about himself).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Many a things are used for the show.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. a thing is.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure "many a" is always followed by a singular noun and a singular verb, even though its meaning is plural.

◦ Structure: Many a + singular noun + singular verb.

◦ Correct: Many a thing is used for the show.

• Hence "a things are" must become "a thing is" — the noun changes to singular ("thing") and the verb to singular ("is").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "a things is" keeps the plural noun "things" with a singular verb — mismatched.

• Option 2 "a things were" keeps both the plural noun and a plural verb — wrong after "many a".

• Option 4 "a thing were" has the right singular noun but the plural/past-subjunctive verb "were"; the sentence is in the present tense, so "is" is required.

NOTE

• Compare the two structures:

◦ Many a student has passed the exam. (singular)

◦ Many students have passed the exam. (plural)

• Similar singular-taking expressions: each, every, either, neither, more than one, one of the + plural noun (the verb agrees with "one").

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can rectify the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to rectify it, select ‘no rectification needed’.

This film is a non-stop riot that many cite as one of the funny films of all time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. funniest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure "one of the ..." is always followed by a superlative degree + plural noun. So "one of the funny films" must become "one of the funniest films".

◦ Structure: one of the + superlative + plural noun.

◦ Correct: This film is a non-stop riot that many cite as one of the funniest films of all time.

• "Funny" is a two-syllable adjective ending in "-y", so it forms its degrees by changing "y" to "i" and adding "-er/-est": funny – funnier – funniest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "no rectification needed" is wrong because the positive degree "funny" cannot follow "one of the".

• Option 3 "more funny" is doubly wrong — the comparative of "funny" is "funnier" (not "more funny"), and a comparative cannot follow "one of the" anyway.

• Option 4 "funnier" is the comparative degree; the structure demands the superlative.

NOTE

• Similar patterns: one of the best players, one of the most beautiful cities, one of the tallest buildings.

• Note also the subject–verb rule: "One of the funniest films is ..." — the verb agrees with "one" (singular).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Transmisible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Transmisible" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "transmissible", meaning capable of being transmitted or passed on (especially a disease). (संचरणीय / फैलने योग्य)

◦ Spelling key: TRANS + MISS + IBLE — note the double "s" (from "transmiss-") and the ending "-ible".

◦ Example: Tuberculosis is a highly transmissible disease.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "Essence" (the intrinsic nature or indispensable quality of something) is correctly spelt.

• "Aggregate" (a total formed by combining several separate items) is correctly spelt.

• "Assembly" (a group of people gathered together; a legislative body) is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Word family: transmit – transmitted – transmission – transmissible – transmitter. The double "s" carries through from "transmission".

• Related confusables ending in "-ible": permissible, admissible, accessible, responsible, feasible. Those in "-able": manageable, comfortable, dependable, reliable.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A person who regards the whole world as his country
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Cosmopolitan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "cosmopolitan" is a person who regards the whole world as his country / who is free from national prejudices and is at home everywhere. (विश्वनागरिक)

◦ The word comes from Greek kosmos (world) + polites (citizen) — literally a "citizen of the world".

◦ Example: Widely travelled and multilingual, he was a true cosmopolitan.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Pacifist" — one who is opposed to war and believes in peace.

• Option 3 "Contemporary" — one who lives at the same time as another; belonging to the present time.

• Option 4 "Celibate" — one who abstains from marriage and sexual relations.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: Patriot (one who loves his country), Chauvinist (one with exaggerated, aggressive patriotism), Xenophobe (one who fears/hates foreigners), Emigrant (one who leaves his country to settle elsewhere), Immigrant (one who comes into a foreign country to settle).

• "Cosmopolitan" is also used as an adjective for a city with people from many countries — Mumbai is a cosmopolitan city.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

The team played / really well, but / they lose the game / in the final minutes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. they lose the game.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a past event — "The team played ... in the final minutes". The verb in the third segment must therefore also be in the past tense: "lost", not the present-tense "lose". This is the rule of tense consistency (sequence of tenses) in a compound sentence joined by "but".

◦ Correct: The team played really well, but they lost the game in the final minutes.

• The past tense of "lose" is "lost" (lose – lost – lost).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "The team played" is correct — "team" is a collective noun taking a singular verb here, and "played" is the correct past form.

• "really well, but" is correct — the adverb "really" correctly modifies the adverb "well" (not "good", which is an adjective).

• "in the final minutes" is a correct prepositional phrase of time.

NOTE

• Do not confuse lose (verb — to be deprived of; rhymes with "choose") with loose (adjective — not tight) and loss (noun).

• When two clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so), they should normally be in the same tense unless the meaning demands otherwise.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

The school shall reopened / after summer / vacations of / one month.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The school shall reopened.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A modal auxiliary ("shall, will, can, may, must, should, would, could, might") is always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb — never by the past form (V2) or past participle (V3).

◦ Wrong: The school shall reopened ...

◦ Correct: The school shall reopen after summer vacations of one month.

• "Reopened" is the past form; after "shall" it must become the bare infinitive "reopen".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "after summer" is a correct prepositional phrase.

• "vacations of" and "one month" are acceptable as printed in the given context.

NOTE

• Modal + V1 examples: He can swim, She must go, They will come, You should study.

• For the passive after a modal use modal + be + V3: The school shall be reopened by the government.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.

They waited with anxiety for the final results.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Calmness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Anxiety" means a feeling of worry, nervousness or unease about an uncertain outcome. Its antonym is "calmness", meaning a state of peace, composure and freedom from agitation. (चिंता / बेचैनी का विलोम — शांति)

◦ Example: They waited with anxiety (worry) — the opposite would be waiting with calmness (composure).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Shrewdness" means sharp practical judgement, cleverness — unrelated to worry.

• Option 2 "Wilderness" means an uncultivated, uninhabited region — a place, not a feeling.

• Option 3 "Feebleness" means weakness, lack of strength — not the opposite of anxiety.

NOTE

• Synonyms of anxiety: worry, apprehension, unease, disquiet, angst, foreboding. Antonyms: calmness, composure, serenity, tranquillity, equanimity.

• Distinguish anxiety (a state of worry) from anxiousness and from eagerness — "anxious to help" can mean "keen to help".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Jack took on three jobs at once but soon realised he had _____________.
option_2: taken it with a grain of salt
option_3: bitten off more than he could chew
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. bitten off more than he could chew.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "bite off more than one can chew" means to take on more work or responsibility than one can handle. Jack accepted three jobs at once — clearly more than he could manage. (क्षमता से अधिक काम अपने ऊपर ले लेना)

◦ Correct: Jack took on three jobs at once but soon realised he had bitten off more than he could chew.

• Note the correct participle form "bitten" after "had" (bite – bit – bitten).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "cut corners" means to do something in the cheapest or easiest way, sacrificing quality.

• Option 2 "take it with a grain (pinch) of salt" means to regard something with scepticism, not to believe it fully.

• Option 4 "play it by ear" means to improvise / act without a fixed plan as the situation develops.

NOTE

• Similar idioms about overload: "have too much on one's plate", "spread oneself too thin", "burn the candle at both ends".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The CEO has _____________ than worrying about individual customer complaints.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. bigger fish to fry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "have bigger (other) fish to fry" means to have more important matters to attend to. A CEO has larger, strategic concerns than individual customer complaints. (अधिक महत्वपूर्ण काम होना)

◦ Correct: The CEO has bigger fish to fry than worrying about individual customer complaints.

• The comparative word "than" in the sentence is the structural clue — only "bigger fish to fry" contains a comparative and fits with "than".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "take a rain check" means to politely decline an invitation now but accept it at a later date.

• Option 3 "throw caution to the wind(s)" means to behave recklessly, taking a big risk.

• Option 4 "walk/skate on thin ice" means to be in a risky or precarious situation.

NOTE

• Related idioms of priority: "first things first", "put something on the back burner" (postpone), "a bigger picture" (the wider view).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Vaccum.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Vaccum" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "vacuum", meaning a space entirely devoid of matter; emptiness. (निर्वात / शून्य)

◦ Spelling key: VAC + U + UM — one "c" and double "u". Learners commonly reverse this and write double "c" with one "u".

◦ Example: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "Perceive" (to become aware of through the senses) is correctly spelt — remember the rule "i before e except after c": receive, deceive, conceive, perceive.

• "Recognition" (the act of recognising) is correctly spelt.

• "Shield" (a protective covering) is correctly spelt — here "i before e" applies normally.

NOTE

• Word family: vacuum, vacuous (empty-headed), vacuity, vacant, vacate, vacation — all from Latin vacuus meaning "empty".

• "Vacuum" is one of very few English words with a double "u"; others include "continuum" and "residuum".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

I know it was wrong to distract his friends, but ________.
option_1: all’s fair in love and war
option_3: all’s unfair in love and war
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. all’s fair in love and war.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The proverb "All's fair in love and war" means in certain intense situations (such as love or conflict) any method, even an unfair one, may be considered acceptable. It is used to justify slightly unscrupulous behaviour, exactly as the speaker does here. (प्रेम और युद्ध में सब जायज़ है)

◦ Correct: I know it was wrong to distract his friends, but all's fair in love and war.

• The saying is attributed to John Lyly's Euphues (1578).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2, 3 and 4 — "all's unfair in the world", "all's unfair in love and war" and "all's fair in the world" — are distorted, non-existent forms of the proverb. Idioms and proverbs are fixed expressions: not a single word may be altered.

NOTE

• Other fixed proverbs commonly tested: "A stitch in time saves nine", "Barking dogs seldom bite", "Every cloud has a silver lining", "Make hay while the sun shines".

question:
Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

(1)___ the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife. I (2)___ she was sleeping late, but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only (3)___ her head, (4)___ something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling. I was glad when the meal was (5)___ and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. At.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "at" is used with the table when we speak of people seated for a meal: "at the breakfast table", "at the dinner table", "at table".

◦ Correct: At the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife.

• "At" indicates a point/position where an activity takes place, which is exactly the sense here — the place where the family gathers to eat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "On" the table would mean placed upon its surface (like a plate or a book), not seated around it.

• Option 2 "Above" means vertically higher than, with no contact — meaningless here.

• Option 3 "Upon" is a more formal variant of "on" and carries the same wrong meaning of resting on the surface.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositional phrases with "at": at the table, at school, at home, at work, at the door, at the top, at noon, at night.

• Compare: The food is on the table (surface) but The family is at the table (seated for a meal).

question:
Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

(1)___ the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife. I (2)___ she was sleeping late, but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only (3)___ her head, (4)___ something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling. I was glad when the meal was (5)___ and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. concluded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Concluded" means arrived at a judgement or opinion by reasoning from the available evidence. The narrator does not see his wife at breakfast and therefore infers that she is sleeping late — an inference, not a decision.

◦ Correct: I concluded she was sleeping late, but Gladolia ... only shook her head.

• The verb "conclude" naturally takes a that-clause: I concluded (that) she was sleeping late.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "accepted" means to receive or agree to something already offered; one does not "accept" a fact one has just guessed.

• Option 2 "decided" refers to making a choice about one's own action; the wife's sleeping is not the narrator's choice to make.

• Option 3 "examined" means to inspect closely — it cannot take a that-clause in this way and does not fit the meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of conclude (in this sense): infer, deduce, gather, surmise, reckon, judge.

• "Conclude" also means "to bring to an end" — He concluded his speech with a quotation.

Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

(1)___ the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife. I (2)___ she was sleeping late, but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only (3)___ her head, (4)___ something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling. I was glad when the meal was (5)___ and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. shook.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed collocation is "to shake one's head", meaning to move the head from side to side to express refusal, denial, doubt or disapproval. Gladolia, when questioned, only shook her head — she would not or could not say anything. (सिर हिलाना — इनकार में)

◦ Correct: ... but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only shook her head, muttered something ...

• The past tense of "shake" is "shook" (shake – shook – shaken), which matches the past-tense narration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "adjusted" (altered slightly to fit) does not collocate with "head" in this sense.

• Option 2 "rotated" (turned in a circle about an axis) is technical and unnatural for a human gesture.

• Option 4 "stirred" (mixed with a spoon / moved slightly) does not go with "head".

NOTE

• Gesture collocations: shake one's head (to say no), nod one's head (to say yes), shrug one's shoulders (to show indifference), raise an eyebrow (to show surprise).

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

(1)___ the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife. I (2)___ she was sleeping late, but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only (3)___ her head, (4)___ something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling. I was glad when the meal was (5)___ and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. muttered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Muttered" means spoke in a low, indistinct voice, often unwillingly or in complaint. This fits perfectly with a servant who refuses to answer clearly, only shaking her head and rolling her eyes. (बुदबुदाना)

◦ Correct: ... only shook her head, muttered something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling.

• "Mutter something" is a natural collocation — the words are unclear, so the object is vague.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "mugged" means attacked and robbed in a public place (or, in Indian usage, learnt by rote) — quite unrelated.

• Option 2 "muffed" means bungled or handled clumsily (muffed a catch) — it does not describe speech.

• Option 3 "mutilated" means severely damaged or disfigured by cutting off a part — far too violent and irrelevant.

NOTE

• Manner-of-speaking verbs often tested: mutter/mumble (speak unclearly), murmur (speak softly), whisper (speak breathily), grumble (complain), stammer/stutter (speak with hesitations), exclaim (cry out suddenly).

question:
Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

(1)___ the breakfast table the next morning, there was no sign of my wife. I (2)___ she was sleeping late, but Gladolia, upon being questioned, only (3)___ her head, (4)___ something, and turned the whites of her eyes up to the ceiling. I was glad when the meal was (5)___ and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. over.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Be over" means to be finished / at an end. "The meal was over" is the standard expression for a meal having come to an end, after which the narrator hurried to the library.

◦ Correct: I was glad when the meal was over and hurried to the library for another try at that story.

• Here "over" functions as a predicative adjective/adverb after the verb "be", which is exactly the slot the blank occupies.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "removed" would mean the meal was physically taken away — it changes the meaning and is unidiomatic here.

• Option 3 "through" would need a subject that is a person: I was through with the meal (✓), but the meal was through (✗).

• Option 4 "undone" means not done / unfastened / ruined — the opposite of finished.

NOTE

• Expressions with "over" meaning "finished": The match is over, It's all over, The worst is over, Game over.

• Contrast "over" (finished) with "over with" (Let's get it over with = finish an unpleasant task).
